title: Standing Homework Instructions
markdown:
## What this covers

This chapter is not built from a lecture. It is the standing instructions that STAT 210A attaches
to every problem set, plus a map of which assignments made up the course across its three recorded
offerings (Fall 2024, Fall 2025, Fall 2026). It belongs at the front of the homework, not inside
any single problem set, because it fixes vocabulary and licence that the individual assignments
rely on without restating: what "numerically" is allowed to mean, what "limiting distribution"
is required to mean, and how casual you may be about measure theory. It assumes only that you are
working through the course's problem sets and want to know the rules common to all of them.

## Conventions that apply to every problem set

Three conventions recur, essentially unchanged, across all three offerings of the course.

**Measure-theoretic niceties are not the point of the exercise, unless the exercise says so.** You
may disregard conditioning on measure-zero sets, the distinction between almost-sure equality and
actual equality, and "all functions" versus "all measurable functions" — unless a problem is
explicitly asking about exactly those issues. The course is about statistics, and a homework
problem that wants you to worry about a null set will say so.

**A numerical answer may always be produced by Monte Carlo.** Whenever a problem asks you to
calculate something numerically, simulating from the appropriate distribution and averaging is
accepted without asking permission first. The obligation shifts instead to precision: a reported
number should be correct to a few significant digits, a comparison between two numbers needs
enough precision for the difference to be meaningful, and a plot of a smooth function should look
smooth. The number of Monte Carlo samples is a judgement call the student makes, not a fixed
recipe.

**A "limiting distribution" means a non-degenerate one, found by centering and scaling.** Unless
stated otherwise, asymptotic statements are limits as $n \to \infty$. If a problem asks for the
limiting distribution of $X_n$, it is not asking for the trivial fact that $X_n$ converges in
probability to some constant — that is a degenerate limit, a point mass, and does not count as an
answer. It is asking you to find sequences $a_n$ and $b_n$ such that

$$b_n(X_n - a_n)$$

converges to a genuinely non-degenerate distribution (not a constant). The standard shape this
takes in the course is the familiar one from a law of large numbers followed by a central limit
theorem — center by subtracting off the deterministic limit, then scale up by the rate of
convergence — but the instruction is general: find *both* $a_n$ and $b_n$, not just the fact of
convergence.

## Submission format

Fall 2026 is the first offering to state a submission format explicitly, as its own heading:
homework is submitted electronically on Gradescope; it need not be typeset in LaTeX and may be
handwritten, unless the problem requires code or figures, so long as it is legible; and code may be
written in any common language (R, Python, Matlab are named explicitly), with anything more exotic
cleared with the GSI first. The underlying expectation was already present in the earlier
offerings without a dedicated heading: show your code if code is needed to answer a question, make
any included plot readable with axis labels and a legend, and expect points deducted for
hard-to-read code or plots.

## How the assignments were organized across the three offerings

The three offerings track each other closely but are not identical.

| Offering | Assignments | Data-backed problems | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Fall 2024 | 11 (Homework 1–11) | Homework 5, Problem 5 (`gibbspoisson.csv`); Homework 10, Problem 3 (`confbands.csv`) | Homework 4 is listed but not linked — its LaTeX source is named with no page behind it. |
| Fall 2025 | 11 (Homework 1–11) | same two data sets, in the same slots | Mirrors Fall 2024 assignment-for-assignment; Homework 4 again listed without a link. |
| Fall 2026 | 12 (Homework 1–12) | Gibbs-sampler data problem moved to Homework 6; confidence-band data problem stayed at Homework 10, Problem 3 | Every homework is linked, including the former gap at Homework 4. The assignment list in the source itself labels the last two entries "Homework 11" twice — the second of the two in fact links to `homework12`, so the twelfth assignment is mislabeled on the page it comes from. |

The actual content of the individual assignments — Homework 1 through Homework 11 or 12 in each
offering — is not part of the material supplied for this chapter; only this index-and-conventions
page was provided, and the assignments themselves are separate pages this page links to.
